display.fanatic_story:
"Do you know how many songs are written out by number up there?" Gus Hartwell asks, pointing at the second floor of the Kerrytown market like it's a lecture hall. "More than 200. Seventeen bells. Anyone can play them. Saturday morning, 10:30 to 11, and I will be at the keys, and I will be playing 'The Victors' until somebody stops me."

"Nobody is going to stop you," Kenzie Rhee says. "That's the problem."

So the UCLA Bruins vs Michigan Wolverines game starts in Ann Arbor with a bell concert, a home finale and a Michigan insider who has turned a free public chime into his personal warmup act. Kenzie, the UCLA insider who storyboards every drive like she's pitching a movie, came east with a script she likes a lot.

"Picture it," she says, framing the Big House with her fingers. "Ten wins. Zero losses. First place in the Big Ten. We go into the biggest stadium in the country on its last home Saturday and we leave with eleven. Roll credits."

Gus clears his throat, which is what he does before he gets technical. "Your movie has had some slow scenes. You beat Oregon 17-15. You beat Wisconsin 17-7. Last week you beat Illinois 22-14. That's not a blockbuster. That's an indie film with good reviews."

"Good reviews win awards, Gus."

This is the strange part of the matchup. UCLA is unbeaten, and the Bruins have won with defense as much as anything, allowing 14.1 points a game. They gave up three at Maryland and none to Nevada. Linebacker Sammy Omosigho has 5.5 sacks and Jalen Woods has 75 tackles. On offense, Wayne Knight is the workhorse, with 845 rushing yards and 13 touchdowns. Ty Dieffenbach has thrown the most passes in each of UCLA's last five games, and last week he found Aidan Mizell for 176 yards against Illinois. Semaj Morgan leads the receivers with 525 yards.

Michigan, under Kyle Whittingham, is 5-5 and fighting for a bowl game. The Wolverines have not won at home since beating Penn State 21-18 on Oct. 17, and after this, the road goes to Ohio State. Whittingham said it plainly after the loss at Oregon: "They better be motivated to make a bowl game."

"We will be motivated," Gus says. "I have done the math, Kenzie. Our defense allows 17.7 points a game. John Henry Daley has six sacks. Troy Bowles has 79 tackles. If we keep you in the teens, we have a chance, and that is not a feeling. That is arithmetic."

"And your offense?"

Gus takes a long pause, the kind a proud man takes when the data is not on his side. Michigan scores 18.3 points a game. The Wolverines completed just six passes at Oregon. Tommy Carr has thrown the most passes in each of the last four games, and Bryce Underwood has six interceptions on the year. Savion Hiter gave the offense a pulse last week with 107 rushing yards.

"Our offense," Gus says, "is a work in progress. A noble one."

Kenzie softens, a little. "I've seen your home games. You beat Western Michigan by one. You beat Oklahoma by seven. You lost to Iowa by one and to Indiana in overtime. Nobody blows you out here."

"Correct," Gus says. "The Big House is where good teams come to sweat."

Here's how it goes. Gus finishes "The Victors" on the chime at 10:59 and gets polite applause from three tourists and a dog. By kickoff, the Big House is loud for its last home game of the year, and Michigan's defense makes the first quarter miserable for everyone. Hiter breaks a long run to set up a field goal. UCLA answers with Knight, again and again, and Dieffenbach hits one deep shot to Mizell for the only touchdown of the first half. Michigan hangs in, scoring on a short field after a Daley sack and fumble. The Wolverines take a late lead, and the students start singing "Mr. Brightside." Then Knight goes to work one more time, and the Bruins kick the winning field goal with under two minutes left.

Kenzie claps her hands together like a clapboard. "And... scene! That's a wrap!"

Gus closes his notebook. "Victors... valiant... later," he says, and heads for the library.

My call: UCLA Bruins 21, Michigan Wolverines 19.

display.story_text:
Santa throws the switch on the evergreen at the Allen Street Gates on Thursday night, two days before Penn State sends off its seniors against Rutgers at Beaver Stadium. The Rutgers vs Penn State spread is a big one, and I'm taking the points with the Over: Rutgers Scarlet Knights +24.5, Over 50.5, with Penn State Nittany Lions 37, Rutgers Scarlet Knights 16 at 3:30 PM ET.

Luann Kessler is already in a holiday mood. "Three straight wins, bowl eligible at 6-4, and we beat Minnesota 42-14 last week. Carson Hansen ran for 126. Rocco Becht has 18 touchdown passes and five interceptions. Tony Rojas leads us in sacks and tackles. Linebacker U is open for business, Vinny."

Vinny Scolari grades it like a boardwalk arm-wrestle. "Lu, we're 2-8, I know. But we lost to youse 40-36 last year. KJ Duff has 774 receiving yards and nine touchdowns. Antwan Raymond has 810 on the ground. We show up."

Penn State has won all nine meetings since 2016, but 24.5 is a lot of football. Three of Penn State's six wins came by more than that, against Marshall, Buffalo and Minnesota. The other three came by 18 at Temple, 14 against Purdue and three at Washington. Penn State's offense scores 30.2 points a game, and my 37 is a good day, not a historic one. Rutgers has lost by more than 24.5 three times, to Indiana, Northwestern and Nebraska. It also lost to USC by seven and Michigan by seven. My 21-point margin sits three and a half points inside the number.

The risk is right there in the box scores. Rutgers was shut out 31-0 by Nebraska last week, and AJ Surace went 4 for 12 for 24 yards with two interceptions. Surace has thrown the most passes in each of the last four games. The Scarlet Knights allow 32.3 points a game.

DraftKings opened Penn State −20.5 and 49.5, as shown in ESPN pickcenter. The side has moved four points toward Penn State and the total is up a point to 50.5.

The Over is where Rutgers' defense helps me. Six of Rutgers' ten games went over 50.5, including 42-35 against USC and 37-30 at Maryland. Four of Penn State's did. My 53 needs Penn State's offense to keep scoring and Rutgers to find two or three drives with Duff and Raymond.

Most of the room is with Rutgers. The Formula has Penn State 35, Rutgers 16, likes Rutgers +24.5 and goes Over 50.5. Next Man Up has Penn State 38, Rutgers 20, likes Rutgers +24.5 and likes the Over. Letdown Watch has Penn State 38, Rutgers 13, lays the 24.5 and goes Over. In The Trenches has no side and no over/under call on this one. Follow The Money is still waiting on a consensus spread, so its side is pending, and it has no total pick.

Letdown Watch: "Senior Day, a bowl ticket punched, a rival that's lost four straight. This could get ugly."

Next Man Up: "Big Senior Day leads mean backups in the fourth. Backups don't stop KJ Duff."

Santa gets one switch to flip in State College this week. Penn State needs a lot more than one big play to win by four touchdowns.

display.fanatic_story:
Luann Kessler has a plan for Thursday night, and it starts at 5 p.m. sharp in MLK Plaza. "Santa arrives at five," she says, counting it off on her fingers like a volleyball rotation. "Light show at seven. And at 7:30, Santa and one lucky kid light the evergreen at the Allen Street Gates. Then Saturday is Senior Day. Vinny, this is the best week of the year in State College."

Vinny Scolari, who drove in from Exit 9 with a sub on the passenger seat, looks at the schedule like it owes him money. "Light Up Night. Beautiful. Very festive. You know what lights up in New Brunswick? My phone, when people text me the scores."

So the Rutgers Scarlet Knights vs Penn State Nittany Lions game arrives at the end of a holiday week in Happy Valley, with the downtown tree glowing two days before the seniors take their last walk at Beaver Stadium. Luann, a former Penn State volleyball setter who has never met a linebacker she didn't love, is ready to celebrate. Vinny, the Jersey guy who grades every trench battle like a boardwalk arm-wrestle, is ready to argue.

"We're bowl eligible," Luann says. "Six and four, three wins in a row, and we just beat Minnesota 42-14. Carson Hansen ran for 126 yards. Rocco Becht threw three touchdown passes on nine completions. Nine! That's efficiency, Vinny."

"I saw it," Vinny says. "I didn't enjoy it."

Penn State's season had a rough middle. The Nittany Lions started 3-0, then lost four straight, to Wisconsin, Northwestern, USC and Michigan. Since then Matt Campbell's team has won three in a row: Purdue, a 28-25 thriller at Washington and the Minnesota rout that clinched a bowl trip. Becht has thrown for 2,163 yards with 18 touchdowns and five interceptions. Chase Sowell leads the receivers with 635 yards. On defense, Tony Rojas leads the team in both sacks, with five, and tackles, with 71.

"Tony Rojas," Luann says, with a hand over her heart. "That's a Linebacker U linebacker."

Vinny, to his credit, does not pretend. Rutgers is 2-8. The Scarlet Knights lost to UMass in the opener. They have lost four straight since winning at Maryland 37-30, and last week Nebraska shut them out, 31-0, in Piscataway. AJ Surace has thrown the most passes in each of the last four games, and last week he went 4 for 12 for 24 yards.

"Fuhgeddaboudit," Vinny says, and then he can't. "Okay, I'm still thinking about it."

But Vinny has his guys, and he lists them with the pride of a man ordering for the whole table. KJ Duff has 774 receiving yards and nine touchdown catches. Antwan Raymond has 810 rushing yards. Dylan Lonergan, who started the year at quarterback, has 10 touchdown passes.

"And here's the best part," Vinny says, sliding his chair closer. "Last year? Forty to thirty-six. We were right there."

Luann smiles the way only a Central Pennsylvania volleyball setter can, sweetly and with menace. "Penn State has won every one of these since 2016, Vinny. Nine in a row. Your best year was losing by four."

"Losing by four is a moral victory in Jersey," Vinny says. "We frame those."

Here's how it goes. The seniors run out of the tunnel to a full Beaver Stadium, and Penn State scores on its first two drives, one on a Hansen run and one on a Becht throw to Sowell. Rutgers answers when Duff gets behind the secondary for a long touchdown, and Vinny stands up so fast his sub hits the floor. Rojas makes two big stops in the second quarter, and the Lions lead comfortably at halftime. In the second half, Penn State keeps the ground game rolling, and the backups get their snaps late. Raymond grinds out a fourth-quarter touchdown for Rutgers to make the final look respectable.

Luann heads to the Creamery and orders a Peachy Paterno, eating it slowly and triumphantly in the cold.

Vinny orders a sub big enough for the whole studio anyway. "For the ride home," he says. "It's a long ride."

My call: Penn State Nittany Lions 37, Rutgers Scarlet Knights 16.

display.fanatic_story:
Vangie Tollefsrud does her Saturday shopping before kickoff, and this Saturday her route runs up University Way NE, where the University District Farmers Market sets up between NE 50th and 52nd Streets from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Rain or shine.

"Apples, mushrooms, a coffee, another coffee," she says, ticking it off while zipping her rain shell to her chin. "Then I walk down to the lake and get in the boat. That's a Husky Saturday."

Mallory Penhallow, who flew in from Bloomington with a garment bag, a laptop and a spreadsheet with forty tabs, looks at the sky like it personally insulted her hair. "How quaint that you have a farmers market, Vangie. In Indiana we have farms."

So the Indiana Hoosiers vs Washington Huskies game kicks off at 12:30 in Seattle with one insider holding a bag of apples and the other holding a win probability chart. Washington is making it Salute to Service and Senior Day at Husky Stadium. Indiana is making it another stop on a trip it would like to keep going for a while.

"Nine and one," Mallory says, sunny as a pageant stage. "We allow 12.5 points a game. Tobi Osunsanmi has ten sacks. Ten! Charlie Becker has 950 receiving yards and ten touchdown catches. Josh Hoover has 19 touchdown passes and two interceptions. And we've won all three of our road games."

Vangie sips her second coffee. "And the one you lost?"

Mallory's smile holds, but only just. "Ohio State. 19-15. We don't talk about tab 41."

Indiana is the second-best team in the Big Ten, and the defense is the reason. The Hoosiers have shut out Howard and Western Kentucky and held eight of their ten opponents to 17 points or fewer. Isaiah Jones leads them with 71 tackles. Last week, against USC, Grant Wilson threw the most passes for Indiana and put up 305 yards and two touchdowns in a 27-13 win. Khobie Martin ran for 82 yards and a score.

"So you have two quarterbacks who can throw it," Vangie says. "Great. Fantastic. Love that for you."

Washington's year has been a rowing race with a few crabbed oars. The Huskies started 3-0, then lost to Minnesota by three, at USC by four and to Iowa at home. They won at Purdue and at Nebraska, lost to Penn State by three, and won at Michigan State last week, 21-14. They are 6-4. Demond Williams Jr. has thrown for 1,955 yards with 13 touchdowns and just four interceptions. Chris Lawson leads the receivers with 851 yards, and he caught five balls for 124 yards and two touchdowns in East Lansing. Safety Alex McLaughlin has 73 tackles.

"We lose close ones," Vangie says. "Three by four points or less this year. You know what that means? It means we're right there. Every week. In the rain."

"It means you lose close ones," Mallory says brightly.

The two teams met in 2024, and Indiana won 31-17 in Bloomington. Mallory has that game on its own tab. Vangie has it filed under "it was sunny there, it doesn't count."

"Our weather is a twelfth man," Vangie says. "Bring your Indiana sunshine. We'll see how long it lasts."

Here's how it goes. The seniors and the service members get their moment before kickoff, and Husky Stadium is loud and damp. Washington takes the opening drive down the field and kicks a field goal. Indiana answers with Becker getting free on a deep ball, and Osunsanmi gets to Williams on third down to end the next Husky drive. Lawson catches a touchdown before halftime to keep it close. In the second half the Hoosier defense takes over, Indiana grinds out two scoring drives on the ground, and a late Washington touchdown makes the final look closer than the fourth quarter felt.

Mallory gives the full pageant wave from the visitors' section and reads the win probability chart out loud like an acceptance speech.

Vangie zips her shell back up and walks to the lake. "Good row," she says. "Wrong finish. See you at the market next Saturday."

My call: Indiana Hoosiers 27, Washington Huskies 18.

display.fanatic_story:
The seniors in Norman have already had their day. Back on Sept. 19, before Oklahoma beat New Mexico 14-6, the Sooners walked their seniors out early, because the team's leadership council asked Brent Venables to move Senior Day off the Texas A&M game so it wouldn't get in the way of a big November Saturday.

"Our captains asked for it," Savannah Redbird-Lowe says, adjusting her rodeo-princess sash like it's a medal. "John Mateer, Jake Maikkula, Owen Heinecke. They wanted Saturday to be about football. Coach V said it best: 'This is their senior year. We're gonna honor them the whole year.' That's Oklahoma."

Colt Wendeborn, Texas A&M petroleum engineer and full-time Yell Leader in spirit, nods with great respect. "That is a fine and honorable tradition, ma'am. At A&M, we honor our seniors by standing for the entire game. Every game. All of us."

"You'll have plenty to stand for," Savannah says sweetly. "Mostly your defense."

So the Texas A&M Aggies vs Oklahoma Sooners game arrives at Gaylord Family Oklahoma Memorial Stadium without the pregame ceremony, and without the November stakes anybody imagined in September. Oklahoma is 6-4 and has won three of its last four. A&M is 4-6, has lost three straight and four of its last five.

Colt takes a deep breath, the kind a man takes when he is about to recite something painful. "Kentucky. LSU. Missouri. Alabama. South Carolina. Tennessee. Six losses, Savannah. I have memorized them, like Aggie Muster."

"That's not the same thing at all," Savannah says.

"It feels the same."

The A&M offense has been the problem. The Aggies scored 20 at Alabama, nine at South Carolina and seven against Tennessee. Marcel Reed, a senior, went 9 for 22 for 71 yards last week, and Mike Elko stood up for him afterward, saying the whole offense was "non-functional" and that it was on him, not one kid. Reed has 1,712 passing yards on the year. Rueben Owens II leads the runners with 508 yards, and Isaiah Horton leads the receivers with 397. Freshman KJ Edwards ran in the only Aggie touchdown against Tennessee.

"Coach Elko took the blame," Colt says. "That's an Aggie. Now somebody just needs to score."

But the A&M defense still shows up. The Aggies allow 19.0 points a game, exactly the same as Oklahoma. Ray Coney has 54 tackles and Marco Jones has three and a half sacks. They shut out Missouri State and The Citadel and held Arkansas to seven.

Savannah is not impressed by The Citadel. She is impressed by her own team. Oklahoma beat Florida 23-7 on the road and Ole Miss 24-17 last Sunday. Mateer has thrown for 2,153 yards with 15 touchdowns, and he ran for 70 yards and a score against Ole Miss. Isaiah Sategna III leads the receivers with 628 yards. Heinecke leads the defense with 82 tackles, and Adepoju Adebawore has four sacks.

"We don't win pretty," Savannah admits. "We beat Texas by three. We beat Ole Miss by seven. We beat Mississippi State by eight. But we win."

"That's what worries me," Colt says. "We don't do pretty either. We just don't do the winning part."

Here's how it goes. Memorial Stadium is full and loud. Oklahoma scores first when Mateer runs it in on a keeper. A&M's defense answers with two straight stops, and Coney blows up a third down to get the Aggie section yelling. Owens breaks a long run, and the Aggies tie it before halftime. In the third quarter, the Sooners kick two field goals and Sategna catches a touchdown. A&M gets a late score and gets the ball back once more, but Heinecke makes the final stop, and Oklahoma escapes by a field goal in its last home game of the year.

"Boomer!" Savannah calls out. She waits.

From somewhere across the stadium, a Sooner fan answers, "Sooner!"

Colt, who cannot yell back in good conscience, finds a broom closet near the concourse and practices a silent yell drill, alone, with total commitment.

My call: Oklahoma Sooners 22, Texas A&M Aggies 19.

Twenty-five and a half points is a big ask for a team that has won by more than that only three times all year, and that's my starting point on Northern Illinois vs North Dakota State. The Bison close their first FBS regular season with Senior Day and the Harvest Bowl in the Fargodome. My card is the road team plus the Over: Northern Illinois Huskies +25.5, Over 45.5, with North Dakota State Bison 35, Northern Illinois Huskies 12 at 4:00 PM ET.

Ingeborg "Inga" Halvorsen keeps a ledger for everything. "Eight and two, Nola. Five and oh in the Fargodome. We allow 12.0 points a game. Kelton McCaslin has five and a half sacks. Nathan Hayes has 14 touchdown passes. We won at Hawai'i 21-13 last week."

Nola Brandvik answers with a farmer's shrug. "We're 0-10, Inga. I know. But we lost to Illinois State by four, UNLV by seven and San José State by 11. Telly Johnson Jr. has 660 rushing yards, and DeAree Rogers has 80 catches. We don't fold."

That's the case for the points. North Dakota State's home wins came by 26 over Jacksonville State, 38 over Fordham, 28 over Wyoming, 14 over Nevada and 24 over UTEP. The Bison offense scores 27.4 a game, and in their last four games it scored 31, 16, 31 and 21. Northern Illinois has lost by more than 25.5 only twice, 40-0 at Iowa and 56-21 to Hawai'i. My 35-12 is a 23-point win, two and a half points short of the number.

The risk is obvious. Northern Illinois scored seven points against Nevada last week, and the Huskies allow 35.9 a game. Taron Dickens has eight interceptions, and North Dakota State's defense has two shutouts.

display.fanatic_story:
Yellow is the color in the Fargodome on Saturday. North Dakota State is asking every fan to wear it for the Harvest Bowl, the annual celebration that closes the Bison home schedule, and this year it lands on Senior Day at the end of the program's first season in the Mountain West.

"Harvest Bowl," Inga Halvorsen says, beaming like she just finished bringing in the wheat. "We thank the farmers, we honor the seniors, we wear yellow. It is the most North Dakota afternoon there is. You'll love it, Nola."

Nola Brandvik, who grew up in DeKalb and studied ag science, nods slowly, the way a person nods at a barn sale when the price is too good to be true. "I respect a harvest celebration. Back home, we'd call this time of year 'bringing it in.' This year, we haven't brought much in."

That's an understatement, and Nola knows it. The Northern Illinois Huskies vs North Dakota State Bison game puts a winless team in a dome full of yellow against a team that has made itself at home in its new league right away. North Dakota State is 8-2 and 5-0 in the Fargodome. Northern Illinois is 0-10.

"Oh, yah," Inga says, gently. "That's a tough one."

North Dakota State's first FBS season has gone the way people in Fargo expected it to, which is to say it has gone well. The Bison opened with a 33-7 win over Jacksonville State, beat Air Force 38-32 on the road and shut out both Fordham and Wyoming. They lost close games at UNLV, 13-7, and at New Mexico, 21-16, and have won two straight since, including 21-13 at Hawai'i last week. The defense allows 12.0 points a game. Kelton McCaslin has five and a half sacks and Donovan Woolen has 71 tackles.

"Twelve points a game," Inga says. "That is the kind of number an economist puts on a refrigerator."

Nathan Hayes runs the offense, with 1,807 passing yards and 14 touchdowns. Jackson Williams leads the receivers with 622 yards, and Myles Mitchell leads the runners with 419.

Nola has her own list, and she reads it with the calm of someone who has already made peace with the weather. Taron Dickens has thrown for 2,070 yards with 10 touchdowns. Telly Johnson Jr. leads the runners with 660 yards. DeAree Rogers has 80 catches for 783 yards. Linebacker Jack Murray has 78 tackles.

"And we've been close," Nola says. "Illinois State by four. UNLV by seven. San José State by 11."

"You did," Inga says kindly. "You also gave up 56 to Hawai'i."

"We don't talk about Hawai'i."

"We just beat Hawai'i," Inga says. "So we talk about it a lot."

The Huskies' defense has been the hard part, allowing 35.9 points a game, and last week Nevada beat them 28-7 at home. Johnson ran for only 31 yards in that game. Still, Northern Illinois has scored 17 or more in six of its ten games, so there is some life in that offense.

"Every field has a few good rows," Nola says. "I'm watching Rogers."

Here's how it goes. The seniors walk out to a dome full of yellow, and the Bison take the opening drive straight down the field, with Hayes finding Williams for the first touchdown. McCaslin gets a sack on the next Huskie series, and the Bison score twice more before halftime. Northern Illinois finally gets on the board with a Dickens throw to Rogers in the third quarter, and the small Huskie section stands up and cheers like it's the Fourth of July. North Dakota State adds two more scores, then lets the younger players finish it. A late Northern Illinois field goal makes the final a little friendlier.

Inga claps her mittens together. "Oh, we won! Hotdish for everybody anyway. It's a harvest."

Nola takes out her phone, pulls up a photo of an Illinois cornfield and stares at it for thirty seconds without saying a word.

My call: North Dakota State Bison 35, Northern Illinois Huskies 12.

display.fanatic_story:
The Turkey Toss is back in Spirit Park on Saturday, for the second year, and Dee Broussard intends to be there early with her pearls on. Southern Miss is making its home finale against South Alabama Senior Day and Military Appreciation, and the Golden Eagles are bringing the annual Turkey Toss back to the tailgate grounds outside The Rock.

"Second year," Dee says, with the pride of a former sorority president who has planned a few events herself. "That's how a tradition starts, Azalea. Year one, people show up. Year two, people show up early."

Azalea Fairhope-Grice, Mobile native and Mardi Gras float-builder, is honestly delighted. "A toss! Dee, we are Gulf Coast people. We toss things for a living. Throw me a first down, throw me a turkey, I'll catch either one."

So the South Alabama Jaguars vs Southern Miss Golden Eagles game comes with a tailgate tradition in its second year, a senior class taking its last walk and a list of active and retired military members being honored throughout the afternoon. Southern Miss is also running its Seats for Service campaign, where fans can sponsor a service member's ticket for 15 dollars.

"That's the best thing about this school," Dee says, and then she catches herself. "Well, one of them. The other one is beating South Alabama, which we haven't done in a while."

Azalea fans herself with a program. "Six in a row, Dee. Since 2020."

Dee winces and fixes her pearls. The series has belonged to the Jaguars lately: 42-35 last year, 35-14 the year before and a 55-3 game in 2023 that nobody in Hattiesburg mentions out loud.

This year, the Jaguars arrive at 5-5 and fighting for a bowl game. They beat Troy 27-14 last week, with Trae'von Dunbar running for 153 yards and two touchdowns. PJ Martin leads the team with 639 rushing yards, and Brendan Jenkins leads the receivers with 568. Jared Hollins and Bishop Davenport have both led the team in throws this year, and Hollins went for 321 yards against UL Monroe.

"We score," Azalea says. "Fifty-six at Arkansas State. Fifty-two against UL Monroe. Forty-one against Ohio. We're a parade, Dee. We just keep coming down the street."

"Your parade has been rained out on the road," Dee says. South Alabama is 1-4 away from home, with close losses at Tulane, Marshall and Louisiana.

Southern Miss, under first-year coach Blake Anderson, has had a hard fall. The Golden Eagles are 3-7 and have lost their last two badly, 54-23 to James Madison and 63-31 at Louisiana Tech. But there have been bright spots. Southern Miss beat Louisiana 35-31 at home in October and won 35-21 at UL Monroe the next week. Steven Robinson has run for 876 yards and ten touchdowns. Mario Sanders has 817 receiving yards and caught eight balls for 119 yards last week. Linebacker Mathis Haygood leads the team with 90 tackles, and Jameer Lewis has four and a half sacks.

"Robinson is the real thing," Dee says. "He carried it 174 times this year. That young man has a strong back and a good heart."

"He's very good," Azalea admits. "Our defense will be ready."

That might be the question. South Alabama gives up 30.4 points a game, and Southern Miss scores 26.9. This one could get loud on the scoreboard.

Here's how it goes. The seniors and the service members are honored before kickoff, and The Rock gives them a big ovation. South Alabama scores first on a long Dunbar run. Southern Miss answers with Robinson, again and again, until he punches it in. The teams trade scores into halftime, and Sanders makes a leaping catch for a touchdown that gets the student section on its feet. In the fourth quarter, South Alabama takes the lead on a Martin touchdown. Southern Miss drives into field goal range and makes it close, but the Jaguars recover the onside kick and run out the clock.

Azalea raises both arms like she's riding a float. "Throw me a bowl game!"

Dee fixes her pearls one more time and heads back toward Spirit Park. "There's still turkey," she says.

My call: South Alabama Jaguars 32, Southern Miss Golden Eagles 30.

display.story_text:
Jayden Maiava walks out of the Coliseum tunnel for the last time as a home quarterback Saturday, on a Senior Day that USC is also billing as Fan Appreciation and Los Troyanos day, and the Maryland vs USC spread asks him to win his farewell by more than 17.5. My pick is Maryland Terrapins +17.5 and Under 57.5, and my final is USC Trojans 35, Maryland Terrapins 20.

Sterling Ashworth-Vance, who grew up a few blocks from Exposition Park and narrates every replay like a movie trailer, is ready for the send-off. "In a world where Maiava has 2,835 yards and 21 touchdowns... King Miller has 727 on the ground. We beat Ohio State 30-18 right here." Abby Chesapeake, the Maryland loyalist who carries Old Bay in her purse, isn't flinching. "We've won two straight. Cardell Williams went 21 of 23 against Wisconsin. And we beat you 29-28 the last time we played."

Start with how USC wins. The Trojans are 7-3, and only two of their seven wins came by 18 or more: 39-0 over Fresno State and 49-30 over Louisiana. Against Big Ten opponents they won by 7 at Rutgers, 4 over Washington, 8 at Penn State and 12 over Ohio State. They are also coming off a 27-13 loss at Indiana in which Maiava threw three interceptions. Maryland has been blown out, no hiding it, 54-3 by UCLA and 45-16 at Ohio State, but the Terrapins have played tighter lately: 37-30 against Rutgers, 20-17 against Illinois, then wins at Purdue and over Wisconsin. Chris Durr Jr. has 804 receiving yards and gives the Terps a way to move the ball late. DraftKings opened USC −16.5. I have the Trojans by 15.

The total rests on USC's recent games. Since the Oregon loss, the Trojans have played 25-21, 31-23, 7-24, 30-18 and 13-27, and every one of those finished under 57.5. Luke Wafle and the USC front have kept games from turning into track meets, and Maryland's offense has produced 24 or fewer in five of its last seven. The posted total opened at 56.5 and nudged up. My 55 points stay under.

The risk is Maiava having one of his big days. He threw for 349 against Fresno State and five touchdowns against Louisiana. If Maryland's secondary looks like it did against UCLA, this gets out of hand in a hurry.

The room splits. The Formula, at 35-19, takes Maryland Terrapins +17.5 and likes the Under 57.5. Next Man Up has 40-22 and takes USC Trojans −17.5 and the Over. Letdown Watch, at 39-15, likes USC −17.5 and likes the Under. In The Trenches has USC by only 26-23, likes Maryland +17.5, and doesn't take a total. Follow The Money is waiting on a consensus spread, so its side is pending, and its total is pending too.

Letdown Watch, to In The Trenches: "Twenty-six to twenty-three? At the Coliseum?" In The Trenches: "You gave the Terps 15. I gave them a pulse."

Sterling gets his trailer moment, the seniors get the win and the crowd gets its blankets. Abby just wants the final scene to stay inside the margin.

USC Trojans 35, Maryland Terrapins 20. Maryland Terrapins cover the 17.5. Under 57.5.

display.fanatic_story:
Maryland Terrapins vs USC Trojans is the last home game for Jayden Maiava and the rest of USC's 2026 senior class, and the Coliseum is packing the whole family into one Saturday: Senior Day, Fan Appreciation and Los Troyanos day, all before a 3:15 p.m. Pacific kickoff. Sterling Ashworth-Vance, who grew up within earshot of the Coliseum and narrates every replay like a coming attraction, already has the farewell scene storyboarded, and Abby Chesapeake flew in from the Maryland suburbs with a can of Old Bay in her carry-on to ruin it.

Sterling: Picture it. Golden hour. The seniors walk out of the peristyle end with their families. Maiava waves to the student section. Cue strings.

Abby: Picture this. Twenty-nine to twenty-eight. You remember that one?

Sterling: I've edited it out of my memory.

Abby: Lucky for you, I brought a copy.

That 2024 game is the only meeting between these two in the last decade, and Maryland won it by a point. It's the kind of thing a Terp brings up early and often. But the Trojans who show up Saturday are 7-3 and ranked No. 18, and they have the quarterback who makes their offense go. Maiava has thrown for 2,835 yards with 21 touchdowns. King Miller has 727 rushing yards, and Trent Mosley has 642 receiving yards, including nine catches for 130 last week at Indiana.

Last week is where Abby wants to live.

Abby: Three interceptions at Indiana. Thirteen points.

Sterling: Every great trilogy has a dark second act.

Abby: That was your tenth game.

Sterling: Long trilogy.

Maryland isn't arriving as a pushover, either. The Terrapins are 4-6, but they've won two straight, 34-29 at Purdue and 24-21 over Wisconsin. In the Wisconsin win, Cardell Williams threw the most times and finished 21 of 23 for 183 yards. Malik Washington has thrown for 2,058 yards this season, and Chris Durr Jr. is the real deal on the outside with 70 catches for 804 yards. On defense, Zion Elee has six sacks, and Daniel Wingate leads the Terps with 61 tackles.

Abby: We're the team nobody wants to see in November. Ask Wisconsin. Ask Purdue.

Sterling: We beat Ohio State 30-18 in this building three weeks ago.

Abby: And then you went to Bloomington and fell asleep.

The truth sits in between. Maryland's rough days were very rough: 54-3 against UCLA, 45-16 at Ohio State, 48-23 at Nebraska. USC's defense, with Luke Wafle up front and Deven Bryant leading in tackles, has been tough in the second half of the season. The Trojans held Ohio State to 18 and Indiana to 27, and those were good offenses.

Sterling: The defense is the unsung supporting actor. Wafle gets my nomination.

Abby: You can't nominate everybody.

Sterling: Watch me.

Los Troyanos day matters to Sterling for reasons beyond football. He grew up in a neighborhood where Saturday at the Coliseum meant three generations in one row, and he likes that USC puts a name on that.

Sterling: My abuela still calls it "el Coliseo." She's never once called it anything else.

Abby: My grandmother calls every crab "a disappointment" until she's cracked it. Same energy.

Sterling: That's not the same at all.

Abby: It's the same energy.

What decides it? USC has to protect Maiava from the same kind of afternoon he had at Indiana, and Maryland has to keep Durr involved and hang around long enough to make the Coliseum nervous. The Terps have shown they can win close ones. What they haven't shown is that they can slow down a quarterback like Maiava for four quarters on the road, in front of a crowd that came to say goodbye.

Sterling: Final shot. Maiava kneels, looks up at the torch, credits roll.

Abby: Fine. But I'm sprinkling Old Bay on your popcorn during the credits.

The seniors get their walk, the torch gets lit, and Maryland makes them sweat into the second half before the Trojans pull away.

My call: USC Trojans 35, Maryland Terrapins 20.

display.story_text:
One hundred years and one day after Memorial Stadium was dedicated to the one hundred seventeen Missouri students and alumni who died in World War I, Mizzou hosts Kentucky on its Military Appreciation night, with the crowd asked to wear black for the 6:30 p.m. Central kickoff. The Kentucky vs Missouri spread is short for two teams that have both lost two straight, and I'm laying it: Missouri Tigers −5.5 and Over 48.5, with Missouri Tigers 29, Kentucky Wildcats 22 as my final.

Delphine Arceneaux-Moss, the Mizzou loyalist who announces everything like a breaking bulletin, has her lead written. "Jamal Roberts: 1,133 rushing yards. Nicholas Rodriguez: 105 tackles. We're 4-1 in this building." Rhett Abernathy-Coyle, the Kentucky horse-farm kid who grades football players like yearlings at a sale, likes his own pedigree. "Kenny Minchey has 15 touchdown throws and two interceptions. We won at Texas A&M and at Oklahoma. We've won six of the last eight against you."

The side is about where each team is trending. Kentucky scored 6 at Tennessee and 14 against Florida in its last two, and that offense was carried for weeks by close escapes: 35-34 in overtime at South Carolina and 35-34 in overtime against LSU. Missouri's losses came against Mississippi State, Ole Miss, Texas and Georgia, and at home the Tigers beat Florida 45-17 and Texas A&M 27-6. Roberts gives Missouri a way to grind out a margin when the throwing game stalls. DraftKings opened Missouri −6.5, and it has come down a point. I have the Tigers by seven.

The total is the bigger call. Seven of Kentucky's ten games have gone over 48.5, and six of Missouri's have. Austin Simmons has 21 touchdown throws against three interceptions, and Cayden Lee has 879 receiving yards. Kentucky's defense allows 25.3 points a game, and Grant Godfrey, with 91 tackles, has been busy all year. The total opened at 49.5 and dipped. My 51 combined points sit over it.

The risk is Kentucky's last two weeks being the real Kentucky offense. If Minchey can't move it, Missouri wins 24-10 and the Over dies.

The room is split all over. The Formula has Missouri 28-24, takes Kentucky Wildcats +5.5 and likes the Over 48.5. Next Man Up has the same 29-22 I do, takes Missouri −5.5 and likes the Over. Letdown Watch, at 30-20, likes Missouri −5.5 and takes the Over. In The Trenches likes Kentucky +5.5 and stays away from totals. Follow The Money's side and total are both pending until a consensus spread and total post after Monday night.

Delphine gets her headline, Rhett gets a close one into the fourth, and the black-clad crowd gets to sing in a building that just turned a hundred.

Missouri Tigers 29, Kentucky Wildcats 22. Missouri Tigers cover the 5.5. Over 48.5.

display.fanatic_story:
Memorial Stadium was dedicated on November 20, 1926, so Saturday night's Kentucky Wildcats vs Missouri Tigers game comes one hundred years and one day later, on Mizzou's Military Appreciation night, with the crowd asked to wear black for a building named for the 117 Missouri students and alumni who died in World War I. Delphine Arceneaux-Moss, who reports every Mizzou development like it just crossed the wire, has been counting down to this date for months, and Rhett Abernathy-Coyle drove in from horse country outside Lexington with a garment bag full of black and a Kentucky lapel pin he refuses to take off.

Delphine: Breaking news. The stadium is a hundred years old and one day.

Rhett: That's not breaking. That's a calendar.

Delphine: It's breaking for anybody who hasn't checked the calendar.

Rhett: Fair enough. I'll wear black. I won't wear gold.

The tribute is the heart of the night, and both of them know it. Missouri students and alumni raised the money and did a lot of the labor to build the place, and it was dedicated to the ones who never came home. Mizzou has spent this whole centennial year honoring that, and Saturday is the most fitting night of the bunch.

Then there's the football, and it's tense. Both teams have lost two straight. Kentucky is 7-3 but fell 34-6 at Tennessee and 21-14 at home to Florida. Missouri is 6-4 after losing 34-20 to Texas and 48-21 at Georgia.

Rhett: We needed a breather. We're rested now.

Delphine: You lost to Florida at home. That's not rest. That's a nap.

Rhett has his reasons for hope, and they start with the quarterback. Kenny Minchey has thrown for 2,160 yards with 15 touchdowns and only two interceptions, and before the last two weeks he was winning tight games all over the league: 35-34 in overtime at South Carolina, 35-34 in overtime against LSU, 21-13 at Oklahoma. CJ Baxter has eight rushing touchdowns, and Kenny Darby leads the receivers with 601 yards. On defense, Grant Godfrey has 91 tackles, and Mi'Quise Humphrey-Grace has six sacks.

Rhett: Minchey has the bloodlines. Calm, strong finish, never panics in the stretch. You can't teach that, you breed it.

Delphine: He's a quarterback, not a colt.

Rhett: Everybody's a colt to me.

Missouri's case starts with Jamal Roberts, who has carried it 228 times for 1,133 yards and nine touchdowns. Austin Simmons has 21 touchdown throws and just three interceptions, and Cayden Lee has 65 catches for 879 yards. The defense has teeth too: Nicholas Rodriguez has 105 tackles, and Daeden Hopkins has seven sacks.

Delphine: Developing story. Roberts is going to run the ball forty times.

Rhett: Is that confirmed?

Delphine: Sources close to me say yes.

Rhett: The source is you.

Delphine: I'm very reliable.

The history favors the visitors lately. Kentucky won six of the eight meetings from 2016 through 2023, including 15-14 in 2018 and 29-7 in 2019. Missouri won 38-21 in 2023, the most recent meeting. But the Tigers are 4-1 at home this season, with wins over Florida 45-17 and Texas A&M 27-6, and the lone loss came against Texas.

Rhett: Six of eight. That's a strong sire.

Delphine: And the last one was ours. New bloodline.

What decides it? Kentucky has to find the offense it had in October, and Minchey has to make throws against a defense that will sell out to stop Baxter. Missouri has to keep feeding Roberts and let Simmons choose his moments. The Tigers have the better ground game and are at home in a building that means a lot this week.

Delphine: Final bulletin. Black jerseys in the stands, Roberts in the end zone, and a hundred-year-old stadium that still sounds young.

Rhett: My bulletin says it's close until the fourth quarter.

Delphine: I'll print both. Mine on the front page.

Roberts wears down the Kentucky front, Simmons hits Lee for the big one, and the crowd in black stays loud right to the end.

My call: Missouri Tigers 29, Kentucky Wildcats 22.
